epics.title: Runtime, dependency, and persistence validation increment
epics.outcome: Establishes the first playable engineering candidate: pinned Phaser runtime, browser-startable scene, paddle/ball/brick core loop, and local best-score persistence, reducing the largest runtime/storage uncertainty before full content and FX.
acceptanceCriteria: An exact Phaser version is selected within the approved Phaser direction and recorded as an implementation prerequisite before content work consumes it.
The candidate can be built and restored from pinned dependencies in a clean environment.
It starts in the assigned Chromium desktop target and shows a scene with paddle, ball, and at least one brick without blocking errors.
Mouse X, click launch, and arrow-key alternative control the paddle; wall, paddle, and brick collisions can be observed in a run.
Local best-score write/read is exercised and survives a normal browser reload subject to browser storage behavior.
No profiling, stress-testing, or measured FPS gate is asserted; representative play only needs to remain stable and readable enough to avoid escalation.

epics.title: Core arcade systems and session model
epics.outcome: Implements the full arcade session state model needed for a playable PoC: launch, rally, scoring, multiplier presentation, lives, HUD, ball loss, restart, and persistence wiring without FX or power-ups.
acceptanceCriteria: Score, lives, multiplier presentation, level display, ball rest/launch, rally counting, brick destruction, ball loss, life loss, and immediate restart are implemented as observable game behavior.
Paddle, ball, and brick states remain independent of FX and power-ups; the primary ball and paddle remain the highest visual priority.
Score and multiplier presentation are visible but do not compete with play-field readability.
The run contains no mandatory timers or pressure mechanics that penalize slower reaction beyond core arcade challenge.
The HUD displays score, level, and lives.

epics.title: Eight-level progression and palette journey
epics.outcome: Delivers eight static, clearable levels whose layout and palette communicate the indigo-to-gold progression without scope expansion.
acceptanceCriteria: Eight level definitions exist, each clearable, distinct by layout and palette, and preserving indigo-to-gold progression.
Levels contain no unreachable brick pockets or unfair power-up spawns.
Power-up introduction order can be expressed without additional brick variants, moving bricks, or hazards.
Palette shifts are linked to level progression and do not compromise ball or paddle readability.

epics.title: Four power-up systems and fair acquisition
epics.outcome: Implements multiball, wide paddle, laser, and slow-time so each can be acquired, used, and expired while supporting fair level completion.
acceptanceCriteria: All four power-ups can spawn, be caught, show readable active states, and expire without obscuring the primary ball or paddle.
Multiball, wide paddle, laser, and slow-time support fair level completion and do not make a level unwinnable if missed.
No optional particle intensity, extra option control, or additional option scope is introduced.

epics.title: Procedural visual generation and provenance
epics.outcome: Creates the code-native visual systems required by the accepted procedural asset strategy for all in-game objects, effects, and palette progression.
acceptanceCriteria: Visual content is generated by reproducible code-native or seeded systems for paddle, ball, bricks, power-ups, particles, glow, CRT treatment, and chromatic treatment.
Generated content has declared project-use rights, hash-bound provenance, and deterministic rebuilds from committed generator/configuration data.

The procedural visual direction satisfies accepted art, colour-safety, readability hierarchy, and high-contrast vector/neon intent without requiring externally authored media solely because older brief text names sprites.
Separate specialist ownership for visual generators is justified by discipline work and does not imply additional content scope.

epics.title: Juice and presentation FX pass
epics.outcome: Implements the bounded high-juice FX required for the player promise while preserving readable chaos.
acceptanceCriteria: Particles, screen shake, hit-stop, glow, chromatic aberration, and CRT treatment combining scanlines and vignette are implemented with high-juice defaults enabled at readability-tested levels.
During multiball, laser, slow-time, high multiplier, cluster destruction, and level clear, ball and paddle silhouettes remain legible.
FX are bounded so global FX and selective toggles can reduce presentation while core gameplay and necessary cues remain legible.
No numeric FX caps or profiling gate are required unless observed instability or readability conflict arises.

epics.title: Required pause, options, and accessibility controls
epics.outcome: Implements only the approved user-facing controls for FX reduction and accessibility, avoiding option-scope creep.
acceptanceCriteria: Pause/options provides only the global FX toggle, screen-shake intensity slider, CRT treatment toggle combining scanlines and vignette, and chromatic aberration toggle.
No separate vignette control, dynamic music layer control, particle intensity/density, gamepad, or additional option controls are implemented as acceptance scope.
Brick state, power-up type, and effect state are not communicated by colour alone, and palettes have colour-safety evidence.
Accessibility controls duplicate important cues visually and allow FX reduction without hiding ball, paddle, or state information.

epics.title: Procedural final-quality chiptune and dynamic audio
epics.outcome: Delivers the required hero tracks and dynamic layers through the accepted procedural asset strategy while preserving final-quality and licensing constraints.
acceptanceCriteria: A code-native procedural chiptune pipeline generates four original hero tracks plus rally, danger, and victory dynamic layers.
Tracks are implemented in build with triggering for rally, danger, and victory beats and are balanced against SFX.
Quality is evaluated against the final-quality chiptune direction; placeholders or temporary audio are not accepted deliverables.
Generated audio has declared project-use rights and hash-bound provenance.
Ownership is defined within available specialist/engineering roles; external composer procurement is not assumed by the accepted procedural asset strategy.

epics.title: Colour safety and readability evidence
epics.outcome: Produces the required non-certification evidence that heavy FX and colour progression remain legible and accessible.
acceptanceCriteria: Colour-safe palettes are documented by simulation or review and representative gameplay captures reviewed by the responsible visual/accessibility lead and accepted by the Director.
No formal accessibility certification is required.
Readability is evidenced during key high-impact gameplay states; if conflict emerges, bounded defaults, options, or escalation for material scope/resource conflict are recorded.

epics.title: Acceptance evidence pack and full scope traceability
epics.outcome: Assembles the PoC deliverables and evidence so every accepted source, constraint, non-goal, and mandatory acceptance criterion is traceable for independent review.
acceptanceCriteria: The acceptance evidence pack contains gameplay captures, build notes, option screenshots, colour-safety review, audio review, design review notes, and performance/readability notes; optional H1-H3 notes may be included only without added scope.
Deliverables include the playable Chromium PoC, design specs, procedural visual/FX pack, procedural audio pack, accessibility/options implementation, and local best-score persistence.
Every mandatory accepted source and non-goal is traceable to a deliverable or documented non-goal.
Director review records acceptance without claiming QA approval before independent checks exist.

feasibilityFindings: The largest technical uncertainty is resolved by the first increment: exact Phaser version, clean dependency restoration, browser startup, core paddle/ball/brick input, and local best-score persistence behavior.
Procedural asset generation is feasible only if reproducible generators can meet the accepted quality bar and licensing/provenance rules; no management authority is currently requested.
Heavy FX, high-juice defaults, and the eight-level palette journey are planned as bounded defaults unless observed instability or readability conflict escalates to technical or Director review.
technicalConstraints: Desktop web browser only; Chromium latest stable is the verification target.
Phaser is the accepted engine direction; exact package version and local persistence mechanism are engineering prerequisites, not new management scope changes.
Audio acceptance requires four final-quality original hero tracks and three dynamic layers; placeholders cannot satisfy acceptance.
Asset strategy is procedural with fallback to procedural, and every provided or generated asset must have declared project-use rights and hash-bound provenance.
Required option controls are only global FX toggle, screen-shake intensity slider, CRT treatment toggle combining scanlines and vignette, and chromatic aberration toggle.
60 fps is a normal-play target, not a hard measured gate; profiling or stress-testing is not required unless instability is observed.
No external deadline or budget cap has been recorded; spending, hiring, and release approval remain separate.
openFeasibilityDecisions: No management-authority feasibility decision is currently open. Routine Phaser pinning, persistence selection, procedural asset pipeline design, and bounded FX/readability tuning remain engineering and design work under accepted constraints.

If the procedural audio pipeline cannot meet the accepted final-quality direction without changing asset mode, reducing accepted content, requiring new spend, or changing scope, that would require an explicit Director decision.
